21	
22	\begin{abstract}
23	% Beat 1: Context
24	AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
25	tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow
26	to hundreds of sessions, both human operators and automated analysis
27	pipelines need aggregate views---not just per-execution debugging.

33	equivalent aggregation problem for programs, but they rely on
34	deterministic function names; agent prompts are natural language and
35	cannot be folded directly.
36	
37	% Beat 3: This paper

40	\emph{operation} is a uniform weighted record for any agent activity; an

42	Sessions and spans become optional fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
43	\toolname implements this model with pluggable intent-recognition
44	backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
45	produces flame graphs, pprof profiles, and structured JSON consumable by
46	both developers and analysis agents.
47

49	On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
50	system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
51	(34{,}539 operations), operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work
52	by 90\% versus flat summaries and fragmentation by 45\% versus
53	fixed-session drilldown. Leave-dataset-out mapping achieves V-measure

59	%% ===================================================================
60	\section{Introduction}
61	\label{sec:intro}
62	
63	AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM
64	calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark
65	labels. As agent deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of
66	thousands of calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need
67	to answer aggregate questions: which categories of work consume the most
68	tokens, where do repeated failures concentrate, and how does cost
69	distribute across semantic task families? Existing observability
70	tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
71	Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize
72	events into per-execution timelines and span trees, enabling
73	single-run debugging. But no existing tool provides an aggregate view
74	that folds heterogeneous events across sessions into a cost or frequency
75	distribution grouped by semantic work category.
76	
77	CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame
78	graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples into
79	a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
80	\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
81	Agent traces break this assumption---prompts are natural language, and
82	two prompts expressing the same intent share no characters. We develop
83	this gap and the design requirements it implies in
84	\S\ref{sec:background}.
85	
86	The central insight is that agent observability requires
87	\emph{profiling}---aggregate, cross-session cost attribution grouped by
88	user intent (which we call \emph{semantic} to distinguish from
89	execution-structural groupings like sessions or spans)---not only
90	per-execution debugging, and that the obstacle to
91	applying classical profiler techniques is the nondeterminism of
92	natural-language identifiers. This paper presents \toolname, a profiler
93	that restores aggregate flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The
94	profiler is built on two abstractions: an \emph{operation} (a uniform
95	weighted record for any agent activity) and an \emph{operation stack}
96	(a field projection chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace
97	identifiers are operation fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
98	\emph{Intent recognition}---mapping free-form prompts to stable labels
99	through pluggable backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, or
100	unsupervised clustering)---restores the deterministic-label precondition
101	that flame-graph folding requires.
102	
103	Some existing tools take steps toward semantic grouping: Datadog LLM
104	Observability clusters user messages by
105	topic,\footnote{\url{https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/}}
106	and Laminar extracts structured signals from
107	traces.\footnote{\url{https://docs.lmnr.ai/signals/introduction}} These characterize \emph{input
108	distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions'') but not
109	\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
110	token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
111	aggregation where width represents cost.
112	
113	This paper makes three contributions:
114	
115	\begin{enumerate}
116	\item \textbf{Insight: agent profiling reduces to two abstractions.}
117	  We show that the aggregation gap in agent observability---fixed
118	  session/span hierarchies cannot fold by semantic category---is closed
119	  by combining uniform operation records with query-time stack
120	  projections, once intent recognition restores deterministic labels
121	  (\S\ref{sec:background}--\S\ref{sec:design}).
122	\item \textbf{System: \toolname.}
123	  We implement this model as a Rust CLI with pluggable intent
124	  recognition, four built-in views, and output formats (pprof, SVG,
125	  JSON) consumable by both developers and automated analysis agents
126	  (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
127	\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
128	  We show that semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
129	  that unsemantic views merge (RQ1), that operation-stack profiling
130	  localizes hidden labeled problems with 90\% less work than flat
131	  summaries (RQ2), and that mapping-derived labels agree with
132	  ground-truth annotations on 7/9 public datasets (RQ3)
133	  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
134	\end{enumerate}

137	\section{Background and Motivation}
138	\label{sec:background}
139	
140	\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}
141	
142	Current agent observability tools organize traces around fixed
143	hierarchies. OpenTelemetry represents an execution as a \emph{trace}
144	containing a tree of \emph{spans}, each with a name, duration, and
145	key-value attributes. LangSmith and Langfuse group spans into
146	\emph{sessions} and display them as timelines or waterfall charts.
147	Phoenix and OpenInference add GenAI-specific span types for LLM calls,
148	tool invocations, retrieval steps, and agent reasoning.
149	
150	These models share a structural property: the session or span tree is the
151	skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and spans
152	nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution time.
153	This design is effective for debugging: a developer can locate a failing
154	span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent chain to understand
155	the execution context.
156	
157	\subsection{Why Fixed Hierarchies Cannot Profile}
158	
159	Profiling requires a fundamentally different operation: \emph{folding}
160	events across executions by semantic category so that width represents
161	aggregate cost. Fixed session/span hierarchies obstruct this in three
162	ways.
163	
164	\paragraph{Sessions are boundaries, not categories.}
165	A session groups events by execution, not by intent. A single session
166	may contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases; splitting by
167	session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
168	performing the same task produce two separate buckets that cannot be
169	merged without external logic.
170	
171	\paragraph{Span names are not semantic labels.}
172	Span names describe mechanisms (\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke},
173	\texttt{ChatCompletion}), not user intent (\texttt{review},
174	\texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping by span name tells you how many
175	LLM calls occurred, not which categories of work consumed the budget.
176	
177	\paragraph{Concrete example.}
178	In a real development project, the system effect
179	\texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok} appears 2{,}903 times
180	across 325 sessions. A flat process summary shows a single counter; no
181	existing trace tool can disaggregate these executions by the semantic
182	intent that triggered them. We quantify this disaggregation in
183	RQ1~(\S\ref{sec:eval}).
184	
185	\subsection{Why CPU Profiling Does Not Directly Apply}
186	
187	CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
188	A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
189	weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
190	ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge; width
191	represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
192	\emph{deterministic}: the same code path always produces the same
193	frames.
194	
195	Agent traces break this precondition. As noted in \S\ref{sec:intro}, prompts are
196	natural language and lack deterministic identifiers; tool calls, GUI
197	actions, and process events are named heterogeneously across agent
198	families. Raw event names cannot serve as flame-graph frames.
199	
200	These observations yield three design requirements:
201	
202	\begin{description}
203	\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
204	  Agent traces mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions,
205	  process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a single
206	  record type that can represent all of them without type-specific
207	  objects.
208	\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
209	  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes---by task,
210	  phase, action, session, or dataset---without rebuilding the trace.
211	  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
212	\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
213	  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
214	  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
215	  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
216	\end{description}
217	
218	%% ===================================================================
219	\section{Design}
220	\label{sec:design}
221	
222	The three requirements from \S\ref{sec:background} drive the design.
223	We introduce two abstractions---operations (\S\ref{sec:ops}) and
224	operation stacks (\S\ref{sec:stacks})---that satisfy R1 and R2, and a
225	pluggable intent-recognition mechanism (\S\ref{sec:intent}) that
226	satisfies R3.
227	
228	\subsection{Operations (R1: Uniform Record Type)}
229	\label{sec:ops}
230	
231	A profiler should not distinguish between prompts, tool calls, and
232	process events at the object-model level. \toolname uses a single
233	abstraction: an \operation is a weighted record with string fields and
234	additive measures.
235	
236	Each operation carries string fields (\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent},
237	\texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag}, \texttt{kind}, \texttt{model},
238	\texttt{path}, \texttt{domain}, \texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive
239	measures (token count, duration, occurrence count). A prompt, an LLM
240	call, a tool invocation, a file read, a GUI click, and a process event
241	are all operation records that differ only in which fields are populated.
242	This satisfies R1: the profiler does not need to distinguish event types
243	at the object-model level.
244	
245	\subsection{Operation Stacks (R2: Query-Time Aggregation)}
246	\label{sec:stacks}
247	
248	An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
249	operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack
250	representation:
251	
252	\begin{small}
253	\begin{verbatim}
254	CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
255	Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
256	\end{verbatim}
257	\end{small}
258	
259	\noindent Unlike CPU profiling, where the call stack is determined by
260	execution, the operation stack is determined by the query. The same
261	operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
262	semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory.
263	Changing the fields changes the aggregation without changing the data.
264	
265	This directly addresses the fixed-hierarchy problem from
266	\S\ref{sec:background}: sessions and spans are optional operation fields,
267	not structural skeleton nodes. Including \texttt{session} in the stack
268	produces a per-session drilldown (equivalent to a trace tree); excluding
269	it produces a cross-session aggregate (which no existing trace tool
270	provides). The same data supports both debugging and profiling views.
271	
272	\toolname is an offline, post-hoc profiler: it reads recorded traces,
273	not live events. Runtime capture overhead belongs to AgentSight, the
274	live-capture component (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
275	
276	A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate $\varphi$
277	selects which operations participate, a stack function $\sigma$ maps each
278	operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
279	nonnegative measure. The view formalism supports arbitrary user-defined
280	views; four built-in defaults (Table~\ref{tab:views}) answer common
281	questions:
282	
283	\begin{table}[t]
284	\centering\small
285	\caption{Built-in views. Each shares the same operation set
286	but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}
287	\label{tab:views}
288	\begin{tabular}{llll}
289	\toprule
290	View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
291	\midrule
292	\texttt{tokens} & LLM calls & token count & Budget distribution? \\
293	\texttt{time} & All timed ops & duration (s) & Time distribution? \\
294	\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\
295	\texttt{network} & Net-effect ops & event count & External contacts? \\
296	\bottomrule
297	\end{tabular}
298	\end{table}

301	\centering
302	% \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig-architecture.pdf}
303	\fbox{\parbox{0.93\linewidth}{\centering\small
304	[Architecture: Agent trace files (Codex/Claude JSONL, benchmark JSONL)
305	$\to$ Parser / Importer $\to$ Intent Recognition (regex / LLM / clustering)
306	or Mapping Rules $\to$ Operations with fields $\to$ Stack query
307	$(\varphi, \sigma, w)$ $\to$ Folded stacks $\to$ Flame graph / pprof /

311	Both paths produce operations; the stack query and output are identical.}
312	\Description{Data flow from agent traces through parsing and intent
313	recognition to folded-stack flame graphs.}
314	\label{fig:architecture}
315	\end{figure}
316	
317	\subsection{Intent Recognition (R3: Deterministic Labels)}
318	\label{sec:intent}
319	
320	Operations and stacks handle heterogeneity and flexible aggregation, but
321	folding still requires deterministic frame labels---the precondition
322	that agent prompts violate (\S\ref{sec:background}). \toolname solves
323	this through \emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts to
324	short, stable labels before stack construction.
325	
326	The design uses a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:
327	
328	\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
329	The production default. Rules have the form
330	\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
331	\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
332	and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
333	match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
334	observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
335	iterate until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
336	rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
337	version-controllable.
338	
339	\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
340	For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
341	(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
342	per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
343	Labels are cached; re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.
344	
345	\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
346	TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
347	without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.
348	
349	The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
350	short; long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
351	and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.
352	
353	\subsection{Mapping for Structured Traces}
354	
355	For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
356	already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
357	quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
358	\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
359	before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
360	analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
361	fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.
362	
363	This dual path explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
364	(which need intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need
365	mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
366	stack query works identically on both.
367	
368	%% ===================================================================
369	\section{Implementation}
370	\label{sec:impl}
371	
372	\toolname is implemented as a Rust CLI (Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}).
373	
374	\paragraph{Trace parsing.}
375	The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
376	history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
377	their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span; LLM
378	calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
379	semantic label. This span-based inheritance is how the profiler connects
380	semantic intent to system behavior without requiring runtime
381	instrumentation.
382	
383	\paragraph{Dataset import.}
384	Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL. Mapping rules
385	(inline or via profile spec) derive fields before stack construction.
386	Standard Chrome Trace Event format can also be imported, with
387	non-\toolname protocol fields preserved as operation fields.
388	
389	\paragraph{Output formats.}
390	\toolname produces pprof protobuf (compatible with
391	\texttt{go tool pprof -http} for interactive exploration), folded-stack
392	text (compatible with Brendan Gregg's \texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone
393	SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries. All outputs are deterministic given
394	the same input and profile spec.
395	
396	\paragraph{Relationship to AgentSight.}
397	\toolname is the offline profiling component of the AgentSight
398	observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
399	capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects;
400	\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
401	tools are complementary: AgentSight answers ``what happened during this
402	run'' (debugging); \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across
403	runs'' (profiling).
404

406	\section{Evaluation}
407	\label{sec:eval}
408	
409	We organize the evaluation around three research questions, followed by
410	case studies and a reproducibility check.
411	
412	\paragraph{Evaluation setup.}
413	We use two classes of data. \emph{Real agent sessions}: 325 readable
414	local sessions (198~Codex, 50~Claude, 77~Claude subagent) from a
415	multi-month development project, containing 183{,}714 system
416	observations. \emph{Public labeled traces}: 15 families covering web,
417	mobile, desktop, software, API, and dialogue agents
418	(Table~\ref{tab:datasets}), totaling 47{,}590 operations through

422	OSWorld-Human) provide hidden ground-truth labels for RQ2. No source

450	\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}
451	
452	The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional
453	tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
454	directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
455	\emph{mixed-intent} buckets---buckets containing observations from
456	multiple semantic regions---under different projection choices.
457	
458	\begin{table}[t]
459	\centering\small
460	\caption{Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations
461	from 325 real sessions. All rows preserve the same total weight.}
462	\label{tab:mixing}
463	\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
464	\toprule
465	Projection & Unique stacks & Mixed wt.\% & Residual\% \\
466	\midrule
467	No semantic labels & 11{,}967 & 90.4 & 44.7 \\
468	Session label only & 15{,}027 & 84.4 & 33.4 \\
469	Prompt label only & 24{,}703 & 36.7 & 7.5 \\
470	Session + prompt & 26{,}829 & 0.0 & 0.0 \\
471	\bottomrule
472	\end{tabular}
473	\end{table}
474	
475	Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result on 325 real Codex/Claude
476	sessions. Without semantic labels, 90.4\% of system-effect weight falls
477	into mixed buckets: a flat \texttt{cargo~test} counter shows 2{,}903
478	executions but cannot distinguish whether they came from
479	\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{refactor}, or \texttt{test}
480	prompts. Adding only the prompt label reduces mixed weight to 36.7\% and
481	residual to 7.5\%. The session label alone barely helps (84.4\%), because
482	sessions typically contain multiple intent phases.
483	
484	A concrete example: \texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok}
485	appears under 48 distinct prompt tags. The top tag (\texttt{refactor})
486	accounts for only 32.0\%; the remaining 68.0\% comes from
487	\texttt{review}, \texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and
488	others. A flat summary or process audit merges all of these.
489	
490	As a robustness check, a label-permutation test (1{,}000 shuffles within
491	each session) confirms the separation is not random ($p = 0.001$). The
492	primary evidence is the mixing reduction itself; the permutation test
493	verifies statistical significance. RQ3 evaluates label quality from a
494	complementary angle: agreement with ground-truth annotations on public
495	datasets.
496	
497	RQ1 also tests whether query-time stack selection (R2) adds value
498	beyond flat label grouping. The same two-abstraction model covers all 15
499	public trace families (Table~\ref{tab:datasets}) without type-specific
500	objects. On the four oracle-rich families, the same 13{,}265 operations
501	fold from 9~dataset stacks to 57~phase stacks, 226~semantic stacks,
502	455~action stacks, or 3{,}757~fixed-session stacks by changing only the
503	stack fields. This is not achievable with a flat GROUP BY on a single
504	label: different stack depths answer different questions (task-level
505	budget vs.\ action-level duplication vs.\ session-level drilldown), and
506	the profiler produces all of them from the same operations.
507	
508	The multi-view design is further validated by metric divergence. The
509	\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
510	only 7/10 top prompt categories (Spearman $\rho = 0.623$).
511	\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by
512	tokens.
513	
514	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
515	\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}
516	
517	A profiler is useful if its top groups correspond to real problems: the
518	categories that concentrate failures, safety violations, or wasted
519	effort should appear at the top of the ranked output. RQ2 tests this
520	correspondence. The methodology is analogous to injecting known
521	bottlenecks in a CPU profiler evaluation: public benchmark datasets
522	provide ground-truth labels (failure, safety violation, redundant step,
523	human-task boundary); we hide these labels, run the profiler, rank the
524	resulting groups, and check whether the top groups contain the hidden
525	positives.
526	
527	\paragraph{Benchmark setup.}
528	Six tasks across four datasets: AgentRewardBench looping and
529	side-effect, SATraj-OS unsafe operation, AgentNet incorrect and redundant
530	step, and OSWorld-Human group start. Together: 34{,}539 operations,
531	3{,}699 positives. Six views (flat, fixed-session, dataset-native,
532	raw-action, operation-stack, label-drilldown) and four rankers (width,
533	visible-risk, query-aware, oracle).
534	
535	\paragraph{Localization results.}
536	
537	\begin{table*}[t]
538	\centering\small
539	\caption{RQ2 hidden-label localization (medians across six tasks).
540	Hidden policies serve only as upper bounds. WTFP = work-to-first-positive.
541	``---'' = group count varies by task; no single median is reported.}
542	\label{tab:localization}
543	\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrrrr}
544	\toprule
545	Policy & Hidden & AP & R@5 & F1@5 & Work@5 & R@30\% & WTFP & Groups \\
546	\midrule
547	flat:width & 0 & 0.168 & 1.000 & 0.287 & 1.000 & 0.000 & 1.000 & 1.0 \\
548	fixed-session:query-aware & 0 & 0.348 & 0.023 & 0.043 & 0.016 & 0.356 & 0.004 & 285.0 \\
549	dataset-native:query-aware & 0 & 0.357 & 0.867 & 0.282 & 0.854 & 0.338 & 0.058 & --- \\

551	op-stack:query-aware & 0 & 0.312 & 0.188 & 0.198 & 0.094 & 0.390 & 0.038 & 157.5 \\

557	
558	Table~\ref{tab:localization} summarizes the results. Flat summaries
559	recover all positives but require inspecting everything
560	(Work@5\,=\,1.0). Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive quickly
561	(WTFP\,=\,0.004) but fragments the workload into 285 groups with only
562	2.3\% top-five recall. Operation-stack query-aware profiling inspects
563	9.4\% of the work in the top five groups, achieves 39.0\% budget-30
564	recall, and reduces groups to 157.5.
565	
566	The result is a Pareto tradeoff, not dominance. The comparison also
567	serves as evidence for the two-abstraction model (C1): fixed-session
568	drilldown and dataset-native hierarchy are alternative abstractions that
569	fix the hierarchy at session or dataset boundaries. Operation stacks
570	subsume both as special cases (include \texttt{session} in the stack
571	to recover fixed-session; include \texttt{dataset} to recover
572	dataset-native). On localization, operation stacks improve top-five
573	recall over fixed-session on 5/6 tasks, reduce median group count by
574	45\%, and save 90\% of inspection work versus flat summaries.
575	Fixed-session drilldown retains lower work-to-first-positive on 4/6
576	tasks: profilers and debuggers are complementary. Bootstrap (10{,}000 resamples) and label-permutation
577	(2{,}000 trials) confirm stable AP deltas exceeding the 95\%
578	prevalence/group-size null on all six tasks.
579	
580	\paragraph{Actionability: which configuration knobs explain the results?}
581	
582	Executable profile-spec patches modify stack fields, mapping rules, or
583	rankers, then re-run over the same visible operations. Five of six
584	patches improve AP, top-five lift, and first-positive work (median AP
585	delta 0.038, median top-five lift delta 0.575). Three reusable patterns
586	emerge: (1)~safety/side-effect tasks benefit from field and ranker
587	changes; (2)~step-quality tasks benefit from operation-stack
588	localization followed by fixed-session drilldown for examples;
589	(3)~human-boundary tasks require boundary-derived fields. The rejected
590	OSWorld-Human patch shows that visible rank features alone are
591	insufficient for boundary objectives; folding held-out boundary-derived
592	fields improves AP from 0.240 to 0.258 and reduces groups from 108 to
593	74, with an explicit work tradeoff.
594	
595	Rank-feature ablations identify 7 critical feature rows
596	(\texttt{repeat\_signal}, write-action, \texttt{status=success}) and 3
597	misleading rows. Guided repairs improve AP on 2/3 misleading cases but
598	use offline scored feedback, not an automatic learned ranker.
599	
600	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
601	\subsection{RQ3: How Reliable Is Intent Recognition?}
602	
603	RQ1 and RQ2 assume that semantic labels are useful. RQ3 tests the
604	label-derivation pipeline itself. For structured traces (public
605	datasets), we evaluate the \emph{mapping} path against ground-truth
606	annotations. For free-form traces (real sessions), we evaluate the
607	\emph{intent-recognition} path at the scale and syntax level; quality
608	assessment of the LLM/regex tagger against free-form ground truth
609	remains future work.
610	
611	\paragraph{Scale and syntax validity.}
612	On 325 real sessions, the LLM tagger processes 118{,}021 tag requests
613	(2{,}859 prompt rows, 114{,}837 LLM-call events). Of these, 82{,}886
614	hit the label cache; 35{,}136 are real llama.cpp calls to a local
615	3B-parameter model. Final tag failures: 0. On a fixed set of 300
616	redacted fragments, three model sizes (0.6B, 1.1B, 3B) all produce
617	900/900 syntactically valid outputs; p95 latencies are 23, 18, and
618	31\,ms respectively.
619	
620	\paragraph{Ground-truth agreement on public datasets.}
621	Public benchmark datasets provide native action labels that serve as
622	ground truth for mapping quality. We run a leave-dataset-out evaluation:
623	for each of 9 datasets, we train mapping rules on the other 8 and
624	measure V-measure between the mapping-derived \texttt{phase} field and
625	the dataset's native \texttt{action} labels, plus boundary F1 between
626	mapped phase boundaries and native action boundaries.
627

632	13{,}265 total operations across 9 held-out evaluations.}

651	Table~\ref{tab:vmeasure} shows the results. On 7/9 datasets, V-measure
652	exceeds 0.7, indicating strong agreement between mapping-derived and
653	native labels. The two low-scoring datasets (toolbench, api-bank) have

656	regressions.
657	
658	A supervised boundary-derivation backend further validates the field
659	pipeline. On OSWorld-Human held-out adjacent pairs, a learned boundary
660	predictor achieves F1~0.77, beating the best simple baseline
661	(\texttt{always\_boundary}, F1~0.71). Learned backends beat simple
662	baselines on 4/5 tested boundary families, while AgentRewardBench
663	looping is fully explained by \texttt{repeat\_signal\_change} (baseline
664	F1~1.0). This supports field derivation as a guarded configuration
665	step, not automatic intent discovery.
666	
667	\paragraph{Cross-configuration consistency.}
668	Two mapping-rule variants (differing in API/tool phase precedence) run
669	on the same 13{,}265 operations produce identical V-measure on 7/9
670	datasets; the two divergent datasets (api-bank, toolbench) differ by
671	$\leq$0.17 in V-measure. This suggests that mapping quality is robust
672	to minor rule variations on well-covered action vocabularies. Direct
673	cross-backend comparison between the regex and LLM taggers on the same
674	free-form prompts remains future work.
675	
676	\paragraph{Semantic quality versus syntactic validity.}
677	Syntactic validity does not imply semantic quality. TinyLlama 1.1B
678	achieves high exact-stability (279/300 identical across repeats) but
679	concentrates on a narrow label set, outputting
680	\texttt{localization}/\texttt{localized} disproportionately. The 3B
681	model produces a broader vocabulary (328 unique prompt tags) but includes
682	noisy entries (\texttt{agentsightsm}, \texttt{testcodex}). A
683	display-governance pipeline reduces unique tags from 1{,}546 to 1{,}364
684	through deterministic aliases, raising top-20 support coverage from
685	93.7\% to 95.2\% without overwriting raw tags. This pipeline manages
686	noise but does not establish semantic adequacy---that is what the
687	ground-truth and cross-backend checks above provide.
688	
689	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
690	\subsection{Case Studies}
691	
692	RQ1--RQ3 evaluate mechanism and fidelity quantitatively. This subsection
693	demonstrates the aggregate, cross-session insights that motivate the
694	profiling abstraction---the kind of questions that per-event timeline
695	views structurally cannot answer. We profile the same 325-session
696	development project and report four representative observations.
697	
698	\paragraph{Budget distribution.}
699	The \texttt{tokens} view (Figure~\ref{fig:flamegraphs}) reveals that
700	\texttt{review}-tagged prompts dominate the model budget, followed by
701	\texttt{git}, \texttt{code}, \texttt{edit}, and \texttt{debug}. A
702	timeline of 80{,}000 individual LLM calls cannot produce this
703	distribution without external aggregation. The stack further decomposes
704	each category: under \texttt{prompt:review}, the dominant sub-frames are
705	\texttt{call:llm/code} and \texttt{call:llm/tool}.
706	
707	\paragraph{Cross-session duplication.}
708	The \texttt{files} view shows \texttt{debug}-tagged prompts across
709	different sessions repeatedly accessing the same source files under
710	\texttt{collector/src/}. The flame graph aggregates these into a single
711	wide bar; a timeline shows each as an isolated event.
712	
713	\paragraph{Metric divergence.}
714	The \texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views share only 7/10 top prompt
715	categories. \texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait)
716	but 93rd by tokens; \texttt{benchmark} prompts show the reverse.
717	
718	\paragraph{Path and network auditing.}
719	The \texttt{network} view attributes domain contacts to prompt
720	categories (\texttt{anthropic.com}, \texttt{crates.io},
721	\texttt{github.com}). The \texttt{files} view identifies accesses
722	outside the project root (\texttt{external/home},
723	\texttt{external/tmp}), supporting security auditing.

740	\subsection{Reproducibility}
741	
742	All results are backed by profile specs for deterministic replay. We
743	re-execute 76 tracked specs twice (152 invocations); all produce
744	identical semantic output. Median runtime: 1.6\,s per spec (p95:
745	2.8\,s). Deterministic-output mode stabilizes raw-byte output: 76/76
746	achieve both semantic and raw-byte determinism.
747	
748	%% ===================================================================
749	\section{Related Work}
750	
751	\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
752	Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
753	folded-stack lineage: profiles are weighted samples with location
754	hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
755	pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
756	generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
757	events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
758	\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
759	difference is the domain: samples are agent operations, frames are
760	semantic labels derived from natural-language prompts through intent
761	recognition, and the evaluation scores profiler output against hidden
762	agent-trajectory labels.
763	
764	\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
765	OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
766	spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
767	Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
768	visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
769	AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
770	covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
771	single-execution debugging: timeline views, span trees, and waterfall
772	charts help locate a specific failure. \toolname complements them with
773	cross-session aggregate profiling.
774	Datadog LLM Observability adds topic clustering over user messages, and
775	Laminar Signals extracts structured events from traces. These are steps
776	toward semantic aggregation, but they characterize \emph{input
777	distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions''), not
778	\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
779	token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
780	aggregation where width represents cost.
781	
782	\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
783	AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
784	constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
785	TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
786	semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas argues that outcome leaderboards
787	miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
788	fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
789	\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling: which
790	categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most budget,
791	or generate repeated system effects across sessions.
792	
793	%% ===================================================================
794	\section{Discussion}
795	
796	\paragraph{Profiler and debugger are complementary.}
797	Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks
798	(RQ2). This is expected: debuggers are designed for single-case
799	investigation. The profiler identifies \emph{which categories} deserve
800	attention; the debugger explains \emph{what happened} in a specific
801	case. \toolname supports both by including or excluding session fields in
802	the stack query. A typical workflow starts with the profiler (``review
803	tasks dominate the budget''), then drills into individual sessions to
804	understand why.
805	
806	\paragraph{Agent-as-consumer.}
807	The profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is
808	designed to be consumed by automated analysis agents, not only human
809	developers. The RQ2 ranker strategies demonstrate this pattern: a
810	scoring policy reads profiler output, ranks groups by visible features,
811	and identifies high-cost or high-failure categories. In practice, an AI
812	coding agent can run \texttt{agentpprof --format json}, parse the output,
813	and recommend configuration changes---the same workflow that the
814	regex-rule iteration (\S\ref{sec:intent}) already uses. This positions
815	semantic profiling as infrastructure for agent self-diagnosis, not only
816	for human inspection.
817	
818	\paragraph{Limitations.}
819	The real-session data (RQ1, RQ3, case studies) comes from one developer
820	on one project. RQ2 mitigates this with four independent public datasets
821	containing real agent traces from different research groups, but
822	multi-project and multi-user real-session evaluation would strengthen the
823	generality claim. The evaluation measures label-scored profiler fidelity,
824	not human or agent productivity. A controlled study comparing
825	flame-graph-guided diagnosis against timeline-based diagnosis would test
826	the practical value but is not required for the profiler-mechanism
827	contribution. \toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and
828	operation JSONL; OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse trace imports are
829	engineering work, not design obstacles.
830	
831	%% ===================================================================
832	\section{Conclusion}
833	
834	Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging. The obstacle is
835	that natural-language prompts lack the deterministic identifiers that
836	make flame-graph folding work. \toolname shows that two
837	abstractions---operations and operation stacks---close this gap once
838	intent recognition restores deterministic labels. The evaluation
839	confirms that semantic profiling separates information flat views merge,
840	localizes labeled problems with less work than both flat summaries and
841	fixed-session drilldown, and produces labels that agree with
842	ground-truth annotations across heterogeneous public datasets.
843	
844	The main limitation is single-project real-session data; multi-project
845	evaluation and direct cross-backend tagger comparison are next steps.
846	The most impactful direction is trace-ecosystem integration:
847	importing OpenTelemetry and LangSmith traces as operations would let
848	\toolname profile any instrumented agent without a custom parser.

\begin{document}

\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}

\begin{abstract}
% Beat 1: Context
AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow
to hundreds of sessions, both human operators and automated analysis
pipelines need aggregate views---not just per-execution debugging.

% Beat 2: Problem
Existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span
hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
across sessions by semantic work category. CPU flame graphs solve the
equivalent aggregation problem for programs, but they rely on
deterministic function names; agent prompts are natural language and
cannot be folded directly.

% Beat 3: This paper
We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions once intent
recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition. An
\emph{operation} is a uniform weighted record for any agent activity; an
\emph{operation stack} is a field projection chosen at query time.
Sessions and spans become optional fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\toolname implements this model with pluggable intent-recognition
backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
produces flame graphs, pprof profiles, and structured JSON consumable by
both developers and analysis agents.

% Beat 4: Results
On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
(34{,}539 operations), operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work
by 90\% versus flat summaries and fragmentation by 45\% versus
fixed-session drilldown. Leave-dataset-out mapping achieves V-measure
above 0.7 on 7/9 held-out datasets.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%% ===================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM
calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark
labels. As agent deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of
thousands of calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need
to answer aggregate questions: which categories of work consume the most
tokens, where do repeated failures concentrate, and how does cost
distribute across semantic task families? Existing observability
tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize
events into per-execution timelines and span trees, enabling
single-run debugging. But no existing tool provides an aggregate view
that folds heterogeneous events across sessions into a cost or frequency
distribution grouped by semantic work category.

CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame
graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples into
a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
Agent traces break this assumption---prompts are natural language, and
two prompts expressing the same intent share no characters. We develop
this gap and the design requirements it implies in
\S\ref{sec:background}.

The central insight is that agent observability requires
\emph{profiling}---aggregate, cross-session cost attribution grouped by
user intent (which we call \emph{semantic} to distinguish from
execution-structural groupings like sessions or spans)---not only
per-execution debugging, and that the obstacle to
applying classical profiler techniques is the nondeterminism of
natural-language identifiers. This paper presents \toolname, a profiler
that restores aggregate flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The
profiler is built on two abstractions: an \emph{operation} (a uniform
weighted record for any agent activity) and an \emph{operation stack}
(a field projection chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace
identifiers are operation fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\emph{Intent recognition}---mapping free-form prompts to stable labels
through pluggable backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, or
unsupervised clustering)---restores the deterministic-label precondition
that flame-graph folding requires.

Some existing tools take steps toward semantic grouping: Datadog LLM
Observability clusters user messages by
topic,\footnote{\url{https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/}}
and Laminar extracts structured signals from
traces.\footnote{\url{https://docs.lmnr.ai/signals/introduction}} These characterize \emph{input
distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions'') but not
\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
aggregation where width represents cost.

This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Insight: agent profiling reduces to two abstractions.}
  We show that the aggregation gap in agent observability---fixed
  session/span hierarchies cannot fold by semantic category---is closed
  by combining uniform operation records with query-time stack
  projections, once intent recognition restores deterministic labels
  (\S\ref{sec:background}--\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{System: \toolname.}
  We implement this model as a Rust CLI with pluggable intent
  recognition, four built-in views, and output formats (pprof, SVG,
  JSON) consumable by both developers and automated analysis agents
  (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
  We show that semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
  that unsemantic views merge (RQ1), that operation-stack profiling
  localizes hidden labeled problems with 90\% less work than flat
  summaries (RQ2), and that mapping-derived labels agree with
  ground-truth annotations on 7/9 public datasets (RQ3)
  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

%% ===================================================================
\section{Background and Motivation}
\label{sec:background}

\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}

Current agent observability tools organize traces around fixed
hierarchies. OpenTelemetry represents an execution as a \emph{trace}
containing a tree of \emph{spans}, each with a name, duration, and
key-value attributes. LangSmith and Langfuse group spans into
\emph{sessions} and display them as timelines or waterfall charts.
Phoenix and OpenInference add GenAI-specific span types for LLM calls,
tool invocations, retrieval steps, and agent reasoning.

These models share a structural property: the session or span tree is the
skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and spans
nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution time.
This design is effective for debugging: a developer can locate a failing
span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent chain to understand
the execution context.

\subsection{Why Fixed Hierarchies Cannot Profile}

Profiling requires a fundamentally different operation: \emph{folding}
events across executions by semantic category so that width represents
aggregate cost. Fixed session/span hierarchies obstruct this in three
ways.

\paragraph{Sessions are boundaries, not categories.}
A session groups events by execution, not by intent. A single session
may contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases; splitting by
session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
performing the same task produce two separate buckets that cannot be
merged without external logic.

\paragraph{Span names are not semantic labels.}
Span names describe mechanisms (\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke},
\texttt{ChatCompletion}), not user intent (\texttt{review},
\texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping by span name tells you how many
LLM calls occurred, not which categories of work consumed the budget.

\paragraph{Concrete example.}
In a real development project, the system effect
\texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok} appears 2{,}903 times
across 325 sessions. A flat process summary shows a single counter; no
existing trace tool can disaggregate these executions by the semantic
intent that triggered them. We quantify this disaggregation in
RQ1~(\S\ref{sec:eval}).

\subsection{Why CPU Profiling Does Not Directly Apply}

CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge; width
represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
\emph{deterministic}: the same code path always produces the same
frames.

Agent traces break this precondition. As noted in \S\ref{sec:intro}, prompts are
natural language and lack deterministic identifiers; tool calls, GUI
actions, and process events are named heterogeneously across agent
families. Raw event names cannot serve as flame-graph frames.

These observations yield three design requirements:

\begin{description}
\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
  Agent traces mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions,
  process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a single
  record type that can represent all of them without type-specific
  objects.
\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes---by task,
  phase, action, session, or dataset---without rebuilding the trace.
  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
\end{description}

\section{Design}
\label{sec:design}

The three requirements from \S\ref{sec:background} drive the design.
We introduce two abstractions---operations (\S\ref{sec:ops}) and
operation stacks (\S\ref{sec:stacks})---that satisfy R1 and R2, and a
pluggable intent-recognition mechanism (\S\ref{sec:intent}) that
satisfies R3.

\subsection{Operations (R1: Uniform Record Type)}
\label{sec:ops}

A profiler should not distinguish between prompts, tool calls, and
process events at the object-model level. \toolname uses a single
abstraction: an \operation is a weighted record with string fields and
additive measures.

Each operation carries string fields (\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent},
\texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag}, \texttt{kind}, \texttt{model},
\texttt{path}, \texttt{domain}, \texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive
measures (token count, duration, occurrence count). A prompt, an LLM
call, a tool invocation, a file read, a GUI click, and a process event
are all operation records that differ only in which fields are populated.
This satisfies R1: the profiler does not need to distinguish event types
at the object-model level.

\subsection{Operation Stacks (R2: Query-Time Aggregation)}
\label{sec:stacks}

An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack
representation:

\begin{small}
\begin{verbatim}
CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}

\noindent Unlike CPU profiling, where the call stack is determined by
execution, the operation stack is determined by the query. The same
operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory.
Changing the fields changes the aggregation without changing the data.

This directly addresses the fixed-hierarchy problem from
\S\ref{sec:background}: sessions and spans are optional operation fields,
not structural skeleton nodes. Including \texttt{session} in the stack
produces a per-session drilldown (equivalent to a trace tree); excluding
it produces a cross-session aggregate (which no existing trace tool
provides). The same data supports both debugging and profiling views.

\toolname is an offline, post-hoc profiler: it reads recorded traces,
not live events. Runtime capture overhead belongs to AgentSight, the
live-capture component (\S\ref{sec:impl}).

A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate $\varphi$
selects which operations participate, a stack function $\sigma$ maps each
operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
nonnegative measure. The view formalism supports arbitrary user-defined
views; four built-in defaults (Table~\ref{tab:views}) answer common

\subsection{Intent Recognition (R3: Deterministic Labels)}
\label{sec:intent}

Operations and stacks handle heterogeneity and flexible aggregation, but
folding still requires deterministic frame labels---the precondition
that agent prompts violate (\S\ref{sec:background}). \toolname solves
this through \emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts to
short, stable labels before stack construction.

The design uses a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:

\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
The production default. Rules have the form
\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
iterate until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
version-controllable.

\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
Labels are cached; re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.

\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.

The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
short; long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.

\subsection{Mapping for Structured Traces}

For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.

This dual path explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
(which need intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need
mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
stack query works identically on both.

\section{Implementation}
\label{sec:impl}

\toolname is implemented as a Rust CLI (Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}).

\paragraph{Trace parsing.}
The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span; LLM
calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
semantic label. This span-based inheritance is how the profiler connects
semantic intent to system behavior without requiring runtime
instrumentation.

\paragraph{Dataset import.}
Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL. Mapping rules
(inline or via profile spec) derive fields before stack construction.
Standard Chrome Trace Event format can also be imported, with
non-\toolname protocol fields preserved as operation fields.

\paragraph{Output formats.}
\toolname produces pprof protobuf (compatible with
\texttt{go tool pprof -http} for interactive exploration), folded-stack
text (compatible with Brendan Gregg's \texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone
SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries. All outputs are deterministic given
the same input and profile spec.

\paragraph{Relationship to AgentSight.}
\toolname is the offline profiling component of the AgentSight
observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects;
\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
tools are complementary: AgentSight answers ``what happened during this
run'' (debugging); \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across
runs'' (profiling).

\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}

The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional
tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
\emph{mixed-intent} buckets---buckets containing observations from
multiple semantic regions---under different projection choices.

Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result on 325 real Codex/Claude

primary evidence is the mixing reduction itself; the permutation test
verifies statistical significance. RQ3 evaluates label quality from a
complementary angle: agreement with ground-truth annotations on public
datasets.

RQ1 also tests whether query-time stack selection (R2) adds value
beyond flat label grouping. The same two-abstraction model covers all 15
public trace families (Table~\ref{tab:datasets}) without type-specific
objects. On the four oracle-rich families, the same 13{,}265 operations
fold from 9~dataset stacks to 57~phase stacks, 226~semantic stacks,
455~action stacks, or 3{,}757~fixed-session stacks by changing only the
stack fields. This is not achievable with a flat GROUP BY on a single
label: different stack depths answer different questions (task-level
budget vs.\ action-level duplication vs.\ session-level drilldown), and
the profiler produces all of them from the same operations.

The multi-view design is further validated by metric divergence. The
\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
only 7/10 top prompt categories (Spearman $\rho = 0.623$).
\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by
tokens.

\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}

A profiler is useful if its top groups correspond to real problems: the
categories that concentrate failures, safety violations, or wasted
effort should appear at the top of the ranked output. RQ2 tests this
correspondence. The methodology is analogous to injecting known
bottlenecks in a CPU profiler evaluation: public benchmark datasets
provide ground-truth labels (failure, safety violation, redundant step,
human-task boundary); we hide these labels, run the profiler, rank the
resulting groups, and check whether the top groups contain the hidden

(\texttt{repeat\_signal}, write-action, \texttt{status=success}) and 3
misleading rows. Guided repairs improve AP on 2/3 misleading cases but
use offline scored feedback, not an automatic learned ranker.

\subsection{RQ3: How Reliable Is Intent Recognition?}

RQ1 and RQ2 assume that semantic labels are useful. RQ3 tests the
label-derivation pipeline itself. For structured traces (public
datasets), we evaluate the \emph{mapping} path against ground-truth
annotations. For free-form traces (real sessions), we evaluate the
\emph{intent-recognition} path at the scale and syntax level; quality
assessment of the LLM/regex tagger against free-form ground truth
remains future work.

\paragraph{Scale and syntax validity.}
On 325 real sessions, the LLM tagger processes 118{,}021 tag requests
(2{,}859 prompt rows, 114{,}837 LLM-call events). Of these, 82{,}886
hit the label cache; 35{,}136 are real llama.cpp calls to a local
3B-parameter model. Final tag failures: 0. On a fixed set of 300
redacted fragments, three model sizes (0.6B, 1.1B, 3B) all produce
900/900 syntactically valid outputs; p95 latencies are 23, 18, and
31\,ms respectively.

\paragraph{Ground-truth agreement on public datasets.}
Public benchmark datasets provide native action labels that serve as
ground truth for mapping quality. We run a leave-dataset-out evaluation:
for each of 9 datasets, we train mapping rules on the other 8 and
measure V-measure between the mapping-derived \texttt{phase} field and
the dataset's native \texttt{action} labels, plus boundary F1 between
mapped phase boundaries and native action boundaries.

to minor rule variations on well-covered action vocabularies. Direct
cross-backend comparison between the regex and LLM taggers on the same
free-form prompts remains future work.

\paragraph{Semantic quality versus syntactic validity.}
Syntactic validity does not imply semantic quality. TinyLlama 1.1B
achieves high exact-stability (279/300 identical across repeats) but
concentrates on a narrow label set, outputting

model produces a broader vocabulary (328 unique prompt tags) but includes
noisy entries (\texttt{agentsightsm}, \texttt{testcodex}). A
display-governance pipeline reduces unique tags from 1{,}546 to 1{,}364
through deterministic aliases, raising top-20 support coverage from
93.7\% to 95.2\% without overwriting raw tags. This pipeline manages
noise but does not establish semantic adequacy---that is what the
ground-truth and cross-backend checks above provide.

\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
folded-stack lineage: profiles are weighted samples with location
hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
difference is the domain: samples are agent operations, frames are
semantic labels derived from natural-language prompts through intent
recognition, and the evaluation scores profiler output against hidden
agent-trajectory labels.

\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
single-execution debugging: timeline views, span trees, and waterfall
charts help locate a specific failure. \toolname complements them with
cross-session aggregate profiling.
Datadog LLM Observability adds topic clustering over user messages, and
Laminar Signals extracts structured events from traces. These are steps
toward semantic aggregation, but they characterize \emph{input
distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions''), not
\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
aggregation where width represents cost.

\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas argues that outcome leaderboards
miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling: which
categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most budget,
or generate repeated system effects across sessions.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Discussion}

\paragraph{Profiler and debugger are complementary.}
Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks
(RQ2). This is expected: debuggers are designed for single-case
investigation. The profiler identifies \emph{which categories} deserve
attention; the debugger explains \emph{what happened} in a specific
case. \toolname supports both by including or excluding session fields in
the stack query. A typical workflow starts with the profiler (``review
tasks dominate the budget''), then drills into individual sessions to
understand why.

\paragraph{Agent-as-consumer.}
The profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is
designed to be consumed by automated analysis agents, not only human
developers. The RQ2 ranker strategies demonstrate this pattern: a
scoring policy reads profiler output, ranks groups by visible features,
and identifies high-cost or high-failure categories. In practice, an AI
coding agent can run \texttt{agentpprof --format json}, parse the output,
and recommend configuration changes---the same workflow that the
regex-rule iteration (\S\ref{sec:intent}) already uses. This positions
semantic profiling as infrastructure for agent self-diagnosis, not only
for human inspection.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
The real-session data (RQ1, RQ3, case studies) comes from one developer
on one project. RQ2 mitigates this with four independent public datasets
containing real agent traces from different research groups, but
multi-project and multi-user real-session evaluation would strengthen the
generality claim. The evaluation measures label-scored profiler fidelity,
not human or agent productivity. A controlled study comparing
flame-graph-guided diagnosis against timeline-based diagnosis would test
the practical value but is not required for the profiler-mechanism
contribution. \toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and
operation JSONL; OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse trace imports are
engineering work, not design obstacles.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Conclusion}

Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging. The obstacle is
that natural-language prompts lack the deterministic identifiers that
make flame-graph folding work. \toolname shows that two
abstractions---operations and operation stacks---close this gap once
intent recognition restores deterministic labels. The evaluation
confirms that semantic profiling separates information flat views merge,
localizes labeled problems with less work than both flat summaries and
fixed-session drilldown, and produces labels that agree with
ground-truth annotations across heterogeneous public datasets.

The main limitation is single-project real-session data; multi-project
evaluation and direct cross-backend tagger comparison are next steps.
The most impactful direction is trace-ecosystem integration:
importing OpenTelemetry and LangSmith traces as operations would let
\toolname profile any instrumented agent without a custom parser.

Line 86–91: The thesis sentence has a 48-word parenthetical interruption between subject and verb.** "The central insight is that agent observability requires \emph{profiling}---aggregate, cross-session cost attribution grouped by user intent (which we call \emph{semantic} to distinguish from execution-structural groupings like sessions or spans)---not only per-execution debugging, and that the obstacle to applying classical profiler techniques is the nondeterminism of natural-language identifiers."
